title: Scaling Transformer Energy-based Models For High Quality Image Synthesis

paper.title:
Scaling Transformer Energy-based Models
For High Quality Image Synthesis
paper.abstract: Abstract Energy-Based Models (EBMs) are a flexible class of generative models that decouple probabilistic modeling from the generation process. This decoupling directly enables compositional generation and inference-time scaling, where sample quality can be refined simply by increasing sampling steps. However, severe challenges in high-dimensional sampling and training instabilities with deep architectures have restricted EBMs to low-dimensional regimes. To resolve these bottlenecks, we introduce the Transformer Energy-Based Model (TEM), a scalable transformer energy function operating entirely within a latent space. On top of this backbone, we extract energies at multiple layers and sum them, composing complementary constraints from local texture to global semantics. Furthermore, two components make this high-quality at scale: Positive Representation Alignment (PRA), which supervises TEM’s intermediate representations with a vision foundation model, and advanced sampling strategies that improve sample quality at inference. TEM-XL achieves an FID-50K of 3.82 on class-conditional ImageNet 256 × \times 256 without classifier-free guidance, showing that a contrastive EBM can generate high-fidelity images. On ImageNet 512 × \times 512, TEM achieves an FID-50K of 8.24, demonstrating that the approach scales to higher resolution. We further validate the core promises of EBMs: compositional generation, zero-shot inpainting, and out-of-distribution detection.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Energy-Based Models (EBMs) [ 23 , 11 ] parameterize probability distributions via an energy function that assigns lower energies to more probable samples and higher energies to less probable samples. EBMs provide a flexible and mathematically elegant framework that fundamentally separates explicit generation from probabilistic modeling. Unlike Diffusion [ 18 , 38 ] and Flow [ 24 ] models, which are mathematically constrained to pre-defined generative trajectories governed by carefully designed timestep schedules, EBMs define the data distribution solely through an energy function, entirely decoupling the model from the generative process. This decoupling of the model from the generative process yields profound advantages. First, EBMs decouple learning from inference, allowing the sampling procedure to be chosen independently of model training. This enables flexible test-time compute scaling by increasing the MCMC steps, progressively refining the samples through a deeper exploration of the learned energy landscape. Second, this flexibility enables the composition of different distributions together [ 11 , 9 ] , which can enable zero-shot generation and generalization capabilities. However, despite their theoretical advantages and compositional properties, EBMs have struggled with widespread adoption due to several critical unresolved challenges. First, EBMs face severe vulnerability to the curse of dimensionality: MCMC sampling suffers from poor mixing in high-dimensional spaces, leading to slow convergence and mode collapse. Second, EBMs scale poorly with model capacity. As network depth increases, conventional architectures exhibit severe training instability, making robust optimization exceedingly difficult [ 11 , 10 ] . Consequently, existing EBM research has been largely limited to smaller-scale benchmarks, unable to demonstrate competitive performance on challenging, high-resolution datasets. “zebra” “beach” ⇓ \bm{\Downarrow} composed result Figure 1: High-fidelity ImageNet 256 × \times 256, 512 × \times 512 generation and compositional synthesis by TEM-XL/2. Left: uncurated class-conditional samples from 80 Langevin steps. The two large images are 512 × \times 512 samples and the remaining tiles are 256 × \times 256. Right: compositional generation by summing the energy functions of two independent classes, producing a coherent scene that satisfies both concepts without retraining. In this work, we address these fundamental limitations and demonstrate that EBMs trained contrastively, with negatives drawn from the model’s own MCMC sampler, can generate high-quality 256 × 256 256\times 256 ImageNet [ 6 ] samples through persistent sampling initialized solely from Gaussian noise, achieving performance competitive with strong generative models (Table 1 ). We further validate the core theoretical promises of EBMs by demonstrating compositional generalization as well as flexible inference-time control. Our work addresses the long-standing scalability bottleneck of contrastive EBMs, reestablishing them as a viable contender for high-fidelity image generation. Our key contributions are: (1) A scalable Vision Transformer-based EBM architecture with multiple energy heads that enables stable training at high resolution. (2) A comprehensive training framework encompassing latent space design, representation alignment, and advanced sampling strategies that together achieve state-of-the-art quality images for contrastive energy-based models. (3) Empirical validation of the theoretical advantages of energy-based modeling at high resolution: compositional generation, zero-shot inpainting, and out-of-distribution detection from a single scalar energy.

sections.heading: 3.1 Transformer Energy-Based Models Architecture
sections.text: TEM Architecture. We parameterize the energy function E θ ​ ( x , c ) E_{\theta}(x,c) with a Vision Transformer (ViT) [ 8 ] backbone adapted for large-scale energy-based modeling. Given an input x x , we tokenize it into spatial patch embeddings, which are processed through a stack of transformer blocks. The final patch tokens are aggregated via global average pooling and passed through a small MLP head to produce a scalar energy E θ ​ ( x , c ) E_{\theta}(x,c) . Our architecture adopts several modern design choices for stability and expressivity. We encode spatial structure with rotary positional embeddings [ 39 ] , and apply query-key normalization [ 15 ] to stabilize attention logits at scale. Feed-forward layers use SwiGLU activations [ 36 ] , and the conditioning signal is projected into feature-wise affine parameters in an AdaLN-style formulation [ 33 ] built on the same RMSNorm variant. Importantly, this design demonstrates stable and effective energy-based modeling at scale without requiring EBM specific components such as spectral normalization commonly used in prior energy-based models [ 11 ] . Multi-layer Energy Extraction. Energy-based models are naturally suited to composition, since combining distributions amounts to addition in energy space. Du et al. [10] demonstrate this by composing several separately trained models, each capturing a distinct concept. Composition of this kind has so far required multiple models. We show that it can instead be obtained within one, extracting energies through multiple heads attached to representations at different depths of a single Transformer. Its layers encode progressively more abstract features, from low-level structure in early layers to high-level semantics in deeper ones [ 34 ] . For L L depth layer with k k heads, we attach them at the blocks nearest to ( L / k L/k , 2 ​ L / k 2L/k , …, L L ). The resulting heads form a hierarchy of energy terms, each enforcing the structure visible at its depth. We train on the sum of these energies, allowing each layer to contribute at its own level of abstraction. This not only yields a better energy function but also decomposes the generative process across layers, opening the way to understanding each layer’s role and further applications.

The first term drives the sampler toward low-energy regions. The second is an entropy term, estimated with a nearest-neighbor statistic [ 2 ] , that keeps its outputs diverse. Together, these terms encourage low-energy, diverse sampler outputs. Appendix A , B gives the details and reports training settings. Representation Supervision. Contrastive EBM training provides only a scalar supervisory signal per sample, one energy value, which makes representation learning challenging at high resolution. A natural remedy is to supply a dense signal to the representation itself, as in diffusion models, where aligning generative features with those of a pretrained vision foundation model (VFM) substantially improves sample quality [ 48 , 43 ] . We study how such alignment should be formulated for energy-based models and introduce Positive Representation Alignment (PRA), an objective designed for the contrastive setting. Let h ¯ VFM ​ ( x + ) ∈ ℝ N × D \bar{h}_{\mathrm{VFM}}(x^{+})\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D} denote the spatially normalized patch-wise output of the VFM, where N N is the number of patches and D D is the embedding dimension. Let h θ ​ ( z + ) h_{\theta}(z^{+}) denote the internal representation of the EBM and P ϕ ​ ( ⋅ ) P_{\phi}(\cdot) a learnable projection network. PRA maximizes the patch-wise cosine similarity between the projected EBM features and the VFM targets: ℒ PRA ( θ , P ϕ ) := − 1 N ∑ n = 1 N sim ( h ¯ VFM ( x + ) [ n ] , P ϕ ( h θ ( z + ) ) [ n ] ) . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PRA}}(\theta,P_{\phi}):=-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\mathrm{sim}\!\left(\bar{h}_{\mathrm{VFM}}(x^{+})_{[n]},\,P_{\phi}\big(h_{\theta}(z^{+})\big)_{[n]}\right). (6) We apply this alignment loss only to positive (data) samples, and never to MCMC negatives. Two complementary intuitions motivate this choice. From a contrastive learning view, alignment acts as a shaping term on the low-energy side of the landscape, while the objective is simultaneously driving negatives toward high energy. Aligning negatives would therefore pull them back toward the data manifold in feature space, working directly against that push. From a manifold view, the VFM produces meaningful features only for inputs near the natural-data manifold. MCMC negatives are typically off-manifold, and this is most pronounced early in training and at intermediate sampling steps, so their embeddings provide no reliable semantic target to align against. This positive-only design also clarifies how PRA is both similar and different to representation alignment in diffusion models, where the distinction lies in what each network receives as input. That line of work aligns the features of a noisy input x t x_{t} with the VFM features of its clean counterpart x 0 x_{0} ; the clean target is dynamic and guides the denoising trajectory toward the data manifold. In our setting both the EBM and the VFM receive the same clean input x + x^{+} , so PRA does not guide any sampling trajectory. Instead it shapes the geometry of the low-energy region of the landscape directly, PRA encourages semantically structured representations of positive samples. Overall Objective. Combining the contrastive energy objective (Eq. 4 ), the sampler matching term (Eq. 5 ), and the representation alignment loss (Eq. 6 ), the full training objective is: ℒ total = ℒ contrast + λ 1 ​ ℒ sampler-match + λ 2 ​ ℒ PRA , \mathcal{L}_{\text{total}}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{contrast}}+\lambda_{1}\mathcal{L}_{\text{sampler-match}}+\lambda_{2}\mathcal{L}_{\text{PRA}}, (7) where λ 1 \lambda_{1} and λ 2 \lambda_{2} are coefficients for each loss. Each term plays a distinct role: ℒ contrast \mathcal{L}_{\text{contrast}} shapes the energy landscape by pushing data samples to low energy and sampled negatives to high energy, ℒ PRA \mathcal{L}_{\text{PRA}} injects semantic structure into the model’s internal representations, and ℒ sampler-match \mathcal{L}_{\text{sampler-match}} encourages low-energy, diverse sampler outputs. The full training algorithm is provided in Appendix D .

sections.heading: 4.1 Main Results
sections.text: Unless otherwise noted, all TEM experiments use batch size 256, learning rate 2 × 10 − 4 2\times 10^{-4} , and 50K iterations, training with 40 steps sampling and inference with 60 steps sampling. Main benchmark numbers for TEM are obtained with inference-time scaling but without classifier-free guidance. All conditions within each ablation are controlled. Full training details are provided in Appendix B . Figure 4: Effect of PRA on training. FID-50K across training steps for TEM-B with no representation alignment, Pos+Neg RA, and PRA. PRA consistently outperforms both, reaching 19.9 FID at 50K steps versus 42.8 without alignment and 36.6 with Pos+Neg RA. This supports aligning only positive samples in our method. Our TEM-XL model achieves a guidance-free FID-50K of 3.82 on ImageNet 256 × \times 256 and 8.24 on 512 × \times 512 (Table 1 ). To our knowledge, these are the best reported large-scale results for a contrastively trained EBM using its own MCMC negatives. Evaluation uses persistent sampling initialized from Gaussian noise and outperforms unguided diffusion transformers of comparable size. This brings contrastive EBMs into the performance range of modern large-scale generative models. Although EBMs are often considered expensive, TEM’s training and inference costs are comparable to, or even lower than, those of diffusion transformers of similar size (Appendix C ). As shown in Figure 3 , TEM scales with model size in both training steps and training compute (left, middle), and scales more steeply than other baselines, overtaking them at the highest budget (right).

sections.heading: 4.3 Test-Time Scaling Analysis
sections.text: We investigate the effect of scaling sampling dynamics at inference time by varying both the number of sampling steps and the step size. Figure 6 visualizes the progressive refinement: at T = 40 T=40 (the training horizon), samples contain residual noise, but extended sampling produces increasingly sharp, class-typical images. Figure 7 quantifies this trade-off. Increasing the number of steps from 40 to 120 and scaling the step size from 500 to 1500 yields higher Inception Scores (indicating more recognizable samples) at the cost of slightly elevated FID (indicating reduced diversity). Notably, this FID-IS trade-off curve closely resembles that of classifier-free guidance, despite requiring no architectural modifications or unconditional network evaluations, but rather just inference-time scaling. This controllability lets users tune sampling to the application, with longer, larger-step trajectories for fidelity and shorter, smaller-step ones for diversity. Compositional generation arises naturally in the energy-based formulation. Let p 1 ​ ( x ) ∝ exp ⁡ ( − E 1 ​ ( x ) ) p_{1}(x)\propto\exp(-E_{1}(x)) and p 2 ​ ( x ) ∝ exp ⁡ ( − E 2 ​ ( x ) ) p_{2}(x)\propto\exp(-E_{2}(x)) denote two energy-defined distributions. Their composition is defined as the product distribution p comp ​ ( x ) ∝ p 1 ​ ( x ) ​ p 2 ​ ( x ) p_{\mathrm{comp}}(x)\propto p_{1}(x)p_{2}(x) , which can be equivalently written as p comp ​ ( x ) ∝ exp ⁡ ( − ( E 1 ​ ( x ) + E 2 ​ ( x ) ) ) . p_{\mathrm{comp}}(x)\propto\exp\!\left(-(E_{1}(x)+E_{2}(x))\right). Consequently, compositional sampling is obtained by replacing the original energy with the summed energy E 1 ​ ( x ) + E 2 ​ ( x ) E_{1}(x)+E_{2}(x) , enabling joint generation that simultaneously satisfies both energy functions. We train TEM-B conditioned on object location and generate compositions of multiple objects at multiple specified positions with CLEVR dataset. Figure 9 shows qualitative samples alongside a comparison against Composable Diffusion [ 25 ] , where we report object detection accuracy for 1-, 2-, and 3-object compositions. Following their evaluation protocol, we train the classifier ourselves using their training recipe. TEM outperforms Composable Diffusion at every composition count. Thus, a single forward pass of E θ ​ ( x ) E_{\theta}(x) directly provides an OOD score without any task-specific training. Our EBM defines a single energy over image latents, allowing refinement from any intermediate completion. We mask the input image before VAE encoding, preventing access to ground-truth content in the missing region. sections.heading: 5 Related Work
sections.text: Foundations of Energy-Based Models. Energy-based models assign an unnormalized scalar energy to each input and define a Gibbs distribution over the data space, an idea with deep roots in statistical physics and undirected graphical models [ 17 , 23 ] . Classical instantiations such as Restricted Boltzmann Machines relied on tractable architectures to make learning feasible, which in turn limited their representational capacity. Du and Mordatch [11] showed that short-run Langevin MCMC combined with a replay buffer yields a practical training loop, producing coherent samples on CIFAR-10. Follow-up work refined the training recipe through improved MCMC initialization, sampler matching terms, and regularization strategies [ 10 , 30 , 29 ] , yet these methods operated at resolutions of 32 × \times 32 or less diverse dataset, leaving the scalability of the paradigm unresolved. Latent-Space Energy-Based Models. Pang et al. [32] proposed training an EBM as a prior over the latent codes of a variational autoencoder, while Hill et al. [16] explored energy-based priors for hierarchical latent variable models. Nie et al. [28] further demonstrated controllable generation by manipulating energies in a learned latent manifold. VAEBM [ 46 ] combines a VAE with an EBM refinement in data space, reparameterizing the MCMC chain through the VAE’s latent space to make sampling practical at higher resolutions. In contrast, we train a single scalar output Transformer energy function in the frozen latent space of a pretrained autoencoder [ 35 ] , keeping the EBM as the sole generative component. Scaling Energy-Based Models. Several recent efforts have pushed EBMs toward higher resolution and stronger performance, though each introduces auxiliary mechanisms that depart from the pure energy-based formulation. EGC [ 14 ] hybridizes energy-based learning with diffusion modeling and can produce 256 × \times 256 ImageNet samples. However, its sampling procedure relies on the full diffusion denoising trajectory. On the adversarial side, Grathwohl et al. [13] reinterpret classifier logits as energies, and Yin et al. [47] scale this idea to ImageNet 256 × \times 256. However, their sampler is initialized from an auxiliary image dataset at both training and inference, and is never seeded from noise at this scale. Trained contrastively, TEM generates high-fidelity 256 × \times 256 images, enabling inference-time scaling and all EBM native applications. Appendix G provides an extended discussion of related work.

sections.heading: 6 Limitations and Conclusion
sections.text: Limitations. TEM’s primary limitation is the computational cost of iterative sampling during both training and inference. One promising direction is to train a feed-forward proposal model to generate candidates in low-energy regions, reducing the sampling needed to refine them. Extended sampling also introduces a fidelity–diversity trade-off: longer trajectories sharpen images but can reduce diversity and worsen FID. Adaptive noise schedules and proposals that enable movement between distinct modes could help preserve diversity while improving sample quality. Conclusion. In this work, we introduce the Transformer Energy-Based Model (TEM), an approach that addresses long-standing scalability issues in contrastive training of energy-based models. With a modern transformer backbone, multi-layer energy extraction, and representation-aware training, we demonstrate that a contrastively trained EBM can synthesize high-fidelity ImageNet images at 256 × \times 256 and 512 × \times 512, competitive with other generative models. We also show that the properties that motivate energy-based modeling in the first place, compositional generation, inpainting, and out-of-distribution detection, remain available at this resolution. We hope this work serves as a starting point for further scaling of contrastively trained EBMs.

sections.heading: B.1 Training Details.
sections.text: The energy head consists of a two-layer MLP with SiLU activations. Details of the transformer architecture are provided in Table 2 . All experiments operate in the latent space of a pre-trained Stable Diffusion VAE [ 35 ] , following Peebles and Xie [33] and are trained with bfloat16 mixed precision. The latent space is clipped by norm 100 to stabilize sampling for 256 × \times 256 and by norm 200 for 512 × \times 512, which is chosen as the threshold containing over 99.99 % 99.99\% of ImageNet training latents, which stabilizes sampling. A smaller threshold clips real data points, while a larger one expands the region the sampler has to search, which slightly degrades performance. For sampling, we use a step size of 500 and noise scale of 0.05. With a small step size, the network would have to produce very large input gradients to move samples meaningfully within a limited number of steps, and we found that this destabilizes training. With an excessively large step size, however, each update is coarse, and the model struggles to learn a fine-grained energy landscape. Following prior work [ 11 , 10 , 12 ] , who likewise decouple the step size from the noise scale and use a step size much larger than the standard Langevin prescription, we select the step size empirically to balance these two effects. During training, 40-step sampling is employed. The replay buffer’s replay probability is set to 0.99 and capacity is 16000. Class labels are drawn independently for every chain, including chains initialized from the buffer. Buffer states therefore serve as class independent initializations near the data manifold, which the conditional energy refines toward the requested class. Once full, each newly added sample replaces a uniformly randomly selected buffer entry. For the sampler matching term, the distance with the nearest neighbor term is calculated based on the distance from 100 randomly sampled seeds to the replay buffer following [ 10 ] . We use DINOv2-large [ 31 ] as the VFM and implement the projection network P ϕ P_{\phi} as a lightweight CNN with spatial normalization following Singh et al. [37] attached after the block nearest to one-third of the total network depth. We use λ = 1 \lambda=1 for energy L2 regularization, λ 1 = 1 \lambda_{1}=1 and λ 2 = 0.6 \lambda_{2}=0.6 for overall objective’s coefficient at Equation 7 following Du et al. [10] and Singh et al. [37] . We optimize the model using Adam with a learning rate of 2 × 10 − 4 2\times 10^{-4} , momentum parameters ( β 1 , β 2 ) = ( 0 , 0.999 ) (\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=(0,0.999) , ϵ = 10 − 8 \epsilon=10^{-8} , and no weight decay. We keep an exponential moving average (EMA) of the weights with decay 0.9999 0.9999 , updated after every optimizer step. All reported samples and metrics use the EMA weights. sections.heading: Appendix C Computational Cost
sections.text: Training the TEM-XL model for 50K steps on ImageNet 256 × \times 256 dataset takes approximately 6 days using 4 H200 GPUs. For sampling, it takes about an hour to sample 50K images with 1 H200 GPU for 60 sampling steps. Higher resolution training on 512 × \times 512 takes roughly 3–4 times longer than 256 × \times 256 on both training and inference.

sections.heading: Training cost.
sections.text: We follow the FLOP accounting convention of Kaplan et al. [22] , letting F F denote the cost of a single forward pass. A standard training step for a diffusion transformer costs 3 ​ F 3F per image: one forward pass and a backward pass of roughly 2 ​ F 2F , since gradients are taken with respect to both the activations and the parameters. sections.heading: Appendix E Compositional Generation in 256x256 CLEVR Dataset
sections.text: To quantitatively evaluate TEM’s compositional performance, we train TEM on a 256×256 location-conditioned CLEVR [ 20 ] dataset consisting of 70,000 images. Prior work on compositional generation evaluates at 128 × \times 128 with a classifier trained at that resolution. We extend this setting to 256×256 to test whether the compositional advantage of energy-based models persists at higher resolution, which is a harder generative setting. The following describes the training setup and the evaluation protocol used to compare against Composable Diffusion [ 25 ] . Training a location-conditioned TEM on CLEVR 256 × \times 256. We train our TEM-B model and evaluate it by providing object locations from real images and composing images according to the number of objects. We condition the energy network on a target object location 𝐩 = ( x , y ) ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] 2 \mathbf{p}=(x,y)\in[0,1]^{2} (normalized image coordinates) through two complementary pathways: a global coordinate code injected by adaptive layer normalization, and a spatial bias added directly to the patch-token grid. To condition TEM on location, we encode each coordinate with a NeRF-style Fourier feature encoding, γ ⁡ ( c ) = [ c , sin ⁡ ( 2 0 ​ π ​ c ) , cos ⁡ ( 2 0 ​ π ​ c ) , … , sin ⁡ ( 2 L − 1 ​ π ​ c ) , cos ⁡ ( 2 L − 1 ​ π ​ c ) ] , \gamma(c)=\big[c,\ \sin(2^{0}\pi c),\ \cos(2^{0}\pi c),\ \dots,\ \sin(2^{L-1}\pi c),\ \cos(2^{L-1}\pi c)\big], (13) which gives a richer positional signal than raw coordinates [ 27 ] . With L = 8 L{=}8 frequency bands, ( x , y ) (x,y) maps to a 2 ​ ( 1 + 2 ​ L ) = 34 2(1{+}2L){=}34 -dimensional code, which is linearly projected, combined with the (optional) attribute embeddings, and injected into every transformer block via AdaLN. We train for 150k steps with batch size 64. Evaluation protocol. Composable Diffusion [ 25 ] operates at 128 × \times 128, and its evaluation classifier is trained at this resolution. We use their released 128 × \times 128 CLEVR checkpoint directly, and train the classifier ourselves following their training recipe with 128 × \times 128 CLEVR dataset. TEM generates at 256 × \times 256, and we downsample its samples to 128 × \times 128 only for scoring, so both methods are judged by the same classifier at the same resolution. The classifier reaches over 99.9% detection accuracy on real 128 × \times 128 CLEVR images, so the reported accuracies reflect generation quality rather than detector error. We report detection success rate over 1,000 scenes for 1-, 2-, and 3-object compositions.

sections.text: TEM as an OOD Detector. TEM provides a scalar energy that we evaluate as an OOD score, using lower energy to indicate more ID-like inputs. We evaluate this property as a secondary capability of TEM. Specifically, we use a TEM-XL model trained with class-label dropout: during training, the class condition is randomly replaced with a null token, allowing the model to learn an unconditional energy function E θ ​ ( 𝐱 ) E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) alongside the conditional one. Each test image x x is encoded to a latent z 0 = ℰ ⁡ ( x ) z_{0}=\mathcal{E}(x) by the Stable Diffusion VAE. [44] . We score DiT using its noise-prediction residual and SiT-based models using their velocity-prediction residuals, with each model’s native interpolation and time convention. All baselines use a single network evaluation, matching the single-forward-pass cost of TEM. For DiT, we use timestep t = 350 t{=}350 . What distinguishes TEM is that the energy provides a single scalar that directly ranks inputs by fit to the learned distribution. Evaluation Protocol. Following Huang and Li [19] , we use the ImageNet-1k validation set (50,000 images) as the in-distribution reference and evaluate on four OOD benchmarks spanning a range of semantic distances from ImageNet: iNaturalist [ 41 ] , SUN [ 45 ] , Places365 [ 49 ] , and Textures [ 5 ] . sections.heading: G.2 Scaling Energy-based models
sections.text: A parallel line of work attains scale by learning energy landscapes from predictive targets rather than from negative samples drawn from the model itself. Du et al. [9] assign a scalar energy to each diffusion timestep via denoising score matching, recovering MCMC-based composition but forgoing a single global energy. Equilibrium Matching [ 42 ] fits a time-invariant equilibrium gradient through a regression objective, defining the energy only implicitly through its gradient field. Its explicit scalar-energy variants (EqM-E) substantially degrade generation quality (FID 73.40 and 75.53 in the B/4 setting). Energy-Based Transformers [ 12 ] learn an energy landscape by backpropagating a reconstruction loss through unrolled inner-loop optimization. Energy Matching [ 1 ] explicitly parameterizes a scalar potential, but achieves its high-fidelity generation results by combining an optimal-transport objective with contrastive energy learning. Its image generation experiments are limited to 32 × \times 32 resolution (CIFAR-10 and unconditional ImageNet 32 × \times 32), so it is not included in Table 1 . In contrast, TEM directly parameterizes a single scalar energy and trains it contrastively using only negatives produced by its own MCMC sampler, without a transport or flow-matching objective. Thus, while prior work demonstrates that energy parameterizations can scale when coupled with predictive, transport-based, or reconstruction-style objectives, our results show that an explicit, contrastively trained EBM can itself scale to ImageNet 256 × \times 256.

This decoupling directly enables compositional generation and inference-time scaling, where sample quality can be refined simply by increasing sampling steps. However, severe challenges in high-dimensional sampling and training instabilities with deep architectures have restricted EBMs to low-dimensional regimes. To resolve these bottlenecks, we introduce the Transformer Energy-Based Model (TEM), a scalable transformer energy function operating entirely within a latent space. On top of this backbone, we extract energies at multiple layers and sum them, composing complementary constraints from local texture to global semantics. Furthermore, two components make this high-quality at scale: Positive Representation Alignment (PRA), which supervises TEM’s intermediate representations with a vision foundation model, and advanced sampling strategies that improve sample quality at inference. TEM-XL achieves an FID-50K of 3.82 on class-conditional ImageNet 256 × 	imes 256 without classifier-free guidance, showing that a contrastive EBM can generate high-fidelity images. On ImageNet 512 × 	imes 512, TEM achieves an FID-50K of 8.24, demonstrating that the approach scales to higher resolution. We further validate the core promises of EBMs: compositional generation, zero-shot inpainting, and out-of-distribution detection. 1 Introduction Energy-Based Models (EBMs) [ 23 , 11 ] parameterize probability distributions via an energy function that assigns lower energies to more probable samples and higher energies to less probable samples. EBMs provide a flexible and mathematically elegant framework that fundamentally separates explicit generation from probabilistic modeling. Unlike Diffusion [ 18 , 38 ] and Flow [ 24 ] models, which are mathematically constrained to pre-defined generative trajectories governed by carefully designed timestep schedules, EBMs define the data distribution solely through an energy function, entirely decoupling the model from the generative process. This decoupling of the model from the generative process yields profound advantages. First, EBMs decouple learning from inference, allowing the sampling procedure to be chosen independently of model training. This enables flexible test-time compute scaling by increasing the MCMC steps, progressively refining the samples through a deeper exploration of the learned energy landscape. Second, this flexibility enables the composition of different distributions together [ 11 , 9 ] , which can enable zero-shot generation and generalization capabilities. However, despite their theoretical advantages and compositional properties, EBMs have struggled with widespread adoption due to several critical unresolved challenges. First, EBMs face severe vulnerability to the curse of dimensionality: MCMC sampling suffers from poor mixing in high-dimensional spaces, leading to slow convergence and mode collapse. Second, EBMs scale poorly with model capacity. As network depth increases, conventional architectures exhibit severe training instability, making robust optimization exceedingly difficult [ 11 , 10 ] . Consequently, existing EBM research has been largely limited to smaller-scale benchmarks, unable to demonstrate competitive performance on challenging, high-resolution datasets. “zebra” “beach” ⇓  m{\Downarrow} composed result Figure 1: High-fidelity ImageNet 256 × 	imes 256, 512 × 	imes 512 generation and compositional synthesis by TEM-XL/2. (6) We apply this alignment loss only to positive (data) samples, and never to MCMC negatives. Two complementary intuitions motivate this choice. From a contrastive learning view, alignment acts as a shaping term on the low-energy side of the landscape, while the objective is simultaneously driving negatives toward high energy. Energy-based models assign an unnormalized scalar energy to each input and define a Gibbs distribution over the data space, an idea with deep roots in statistical physics and undirected graphical models [ 17 , 23 ] . Classical instantiations such as Restricted Boltzmann Machines relied on tractable architectures to make learning feasible, which in turn limited their representational capacity. Du and Mordatch [11] showed that short-run Langevin MCMC combined with a replay buffer yields a practical training loop, producing coherent samples on CIFAR-10. Follow-up work refined the training recipe through improved MCMC initialization, sampler matching terms, and regularization strategies [ 10 , 30 , 29 ] , yet these methods operated at resolutions of 32 × 	imes 32 or less diverse dataset, leaving the scalability of the paradigm unresolved. Latent-Space Energy-Based Models. Pang et al. [32] proposed training an EBM as a prior over the latent codes of a variational autoencoder, while Hill et al. [16] explored energy-based priors for hierarchical latent variable models. Nie et al. [28] further demonstrated controllable generation by manipulating energies in a learned latent manifold. VAEBM [ 46 ] combines a VAE with an EBM refinement in data space, reparameterizing the MCMC chain through the VAE’s latent space to make sampling practical at higher resolutions. In contrast, we train a single scalar output Transformer energy function in the frozen latent space of a pretrained autoencoder [ 35 ] , keeping the EBM as the sole generative component. Scaling Energy-Based Models. Several recent efforts have pushed EBMs toward higher resolution and stronger performance, though each introduces auxiliary mechanisms that depart from the pure energy-based formulation. EGC [ 14 ] hybridizes energy-based learning with diffusion modeling and can produce 256 × 	imes 256 ImageNet samples. However, its sampling procedure relies on the full diffusion denoising trajectory. On the adversarial side, Grathwohl et al. [13] reinterpret classifier logits as energies, and Yin et al. [47] scale this idea to ImageNet 256 × 	imes 256. However, their sampler is initialized from an auxiliary image dataset at both training and inference, and is never seeded from noise at this scale. Trained contrastively, TEM generates high-fidelity 256 × 	imes 256 images, enabling inference-time scaling and all EBM native applications. Appendix G provides an extended discussion of related work. 6 Limitations and Conclusion Limitations. TEM’s primary limitation is the computational cost of iterative sampling during both training and inference. One promising direction is to train a feed-forward proposal model to generate candidates in low-energy regions, reducing the sampling needed to refine them. Extended sampling also introduces a fidelity–diversity trade-off: longer trajectories sharpen images but can reduce diversity and worsen FID. Adaptive noise schedules and proposals that enable movement between distinct modes could help preserve diversity while improving sample quality. Conclusion. In this work, we introduce the Transformer Energy-Based Model (TEM), an approach that addresses long-standing scalability issues in contrastive training of energy-based models. With a modern transformer backbone, multi-layer energy extraction, and representation-aware training, we demonstrate that a contrastively trained EBM can synthesize high-fidelity ImageNet images at 256 × 	imes 256 and 512 × 	imes 512, competitive with other generative models. We also show that the properties that motivate energy-based modeling in the first place, compositional generation, inpainting, and out-of-distribution detection, remain available at this resolution. We hope this work serves as a starting point for further scaling of contrastively trained EBMs. Acknowledgments We thank William Moy for helpful discussion and feedback.
